wiki.extract: The Citadelle Laferrière is a mountaintop fortress built after Haitian independence (1804-1820) to defend against a feared French return. The largest fortress in the Americas and a UNESCO World Heritage Site, it symbolizes Haiti's revolutionary triumph.

Sans-Souci Palace, near Milot, was the royal residence of King Henri Christophe, completed in 1813 as a symbol of Black sovereignty and splendor. Now evocative ruins within the National History Park, it is part of Haiti's UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Labadee is a private resort enclave on Haiti's northern coast leased by Royal Caribbean, offering beaches, water sports, and Haiti's longest zipline over water. It remains one of the few steady sources of tourism revenue for the country.

Jacmel, a port town on Haiti's south coast, is famed for its French colonial architecture, vibrant arts scene, and elaborate carnival masks and papier-mache crafts. Its historic center reflects the coffee boom of the 19th century.

Bassin Bleu is a series of cobalt-blue waterfalls and pools hidden in the hills above Jacmel, reached by hiking through tropical forest. Its strikingly blue basins, colored by minerals, are among Haiti's most beautiful natural wonders.

head_of_state: Acting Prime Minister Alix Didier Fils-Aimé

wiki.extract: Haiti's Kanaval is one of the largest Mardi Gras carnivals in the Caribbean, running from January's Pre-Kanaval through February with massive parades, rara bands, and Vodou-influenced revelry in Port-au-Prince. Celebrations end on Mardi Gras before Lent.

Fête Gede, the Festival of the Ancestors, is a Vodou celebration held November 1-2 honoring Gede, the lwa of death and fertility. Devotees in purple and black gather in cemeteries with rum offerings, drumming, and dancing.

Rara is a series of street processions held during the Catholic Lent season, with bamboo trumpet (vaksen) bands, drums, and dancing crowds parading through towns and countryside. It blends African, Vodou, and Catholic traditions into a uniquely Haitian festival.

The Carnaval des Fleurs (Carnival of Flowers) is a summer carnival held in Port-au-Prince, first launched in 2012 to boost tourism and celebrate Haiti's flora. Three days of parades, music, and elaborate costumes fill the capital in late July.

The Port-au-Prince International Jazz Festival (PAPJAZZ) has run every January since 2007, bringing nearly a hundred Haitian and international musicians for eight days of concerts across the capital. It promotes jazz in Haiti and cultural exchange with the wider world.

food_writeup: Haitian cuisine blends African, French, and Taíno influences, centered on rice and beans (diri kole ak pwa), griot (fried pork), and pikliz, a spicy pickled vegetable condiment. Soup joumou, a pumpkin soup traditionally eaten on Independence Day (January 1), commemorates emancipation, while plantains, yams, and fresh tropical fruit round out the table.
brief_history: Haiti became the world's first Black republic in 1804 after enslaved Africans overthrew French colonial rule in the Haitian Revolution. The 20th century brought U.S. occupation, the Duvalier dictatorships, and chronic political instability; the 2010 earthquake killed over 200,000 people, and since the 2021 assassination of President Jovenel Moïse, gang violence has plunged much of the country into a severe security and humanitarian crisis.
current_conflicts: Haiti is in a severe security crisis: armed gangs control most of Port-au-Prince and large areas elsewhere, displacing hundreds of thousands and crippling the economy. A Kenyan-led multinational security mission deployed in 2024, and the UN authorized an expanded Gang Suppression Force in September 2026, while transitional authorities plan elections.
